turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on back. The desk put down heart racing, but tell me what's actually going on.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, it flutters, or it races, I don't know, doctor. It's hard to describe.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When it races, is that a couple of extra beats, or fast for a whole stretch?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Fast for a stretch. And I get out of breath with it, like I can't fill my lungs.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the breathing start first, or the heart?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Heart first, then the breath. Usually. Well, actually, sometimes they hit together. I don't know.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been happening?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A couple months? I kept thinking it'd just stop.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): My partner says it was already going on back in the winter, but I can't put a date on it. I really don't know.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, no solid start date, we'll leave that open. Is it every single day?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Mostly at night, in bed. And before exams, or before meetings at work. Which sounds silly.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not silly. School, work, or both?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. I'm twenty-three, doing a master's, and I work part-time at a marketing firm downtown. Client meetings are the bad ones.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): At night, do you wake up gasping, or are you still awake when it starts?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Still awake. Just lying there. Heart going, can't catch my breath, and then I kind of... yeah.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with these spells?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain at all.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Passed out? Gotten lightheaded?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fainting, and I'm not lightheaded with these. I don't know, doctor, it just feels like I can't get air.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, no fainting and no lightheaded spells with it. How long does an episode last?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Five minutes, sometimes twenty. I never time it, so that's a guess.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee, soda, energy drinks — what's a normal day?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): A lot of coffee. Four, well actually five cups. And two Monsters if there's a deadline. My partner swears that's the whole thing.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): They might be onto something, but I'm not pinning it there yet. Do you smoke or vape?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. Not cigarettes. The disposable nicotine ones. A pod every couple of days, more when I'm cramming. Is that bad?
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Enough nicotine to push the heart rate up, yes. Any alcohol?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): A beer on the weekend sometimes. That's it. Oh, and your parking garage almost made me late, I circled forever.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): That garage gets everyone. People will call this anxiety — do you feel stressed or panicky when the racing starts?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. I don't think it's that. Exams are just exams. I don't know why everyone jumps to anxiety.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're telling me it isn't stress, so that's what I'll write. Thinking out loud, though, the timing with meetings still nags at me. Any medicine you've used for the racing?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Propranolol. They started it last fall, ten milligrams once a day, by mouth, for the heart racing.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you still taking that?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I stopped it in March. It made me tired, and I don't know, I didn't feel like it was doing anything.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair. Anything else that got prescribed and never actually started?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Buspirone, for nerves. I never filled it. Never took one pill. Which, I'm not anxious, so.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then buspirone stays off the list. Anything at all in your system now — vitamins, somebody else's pill?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No vitamins. I took one of my roommate's Adderall before a final, months ago, just once. Not my prescription, and I didn't do it again.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): One-time use of someone else's Adderall doesn't go on your medication list. Drug allergies, or allergies to anything else?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe penicillin, or that might be my brother, I always mix us up. I can't remember a rash or what happened.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we'll call penicillin uncertain, not a confirmed allergy. Any diagnosed problems — asthma, thyroid disease, a heart condition?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing like that. No asthma. Nobody ever said I had a thyroid problem. Never had surgery, either.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family history — rhythm problems, heart disease, high blood pressure?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know about rhythm stuff. My dad has high blood pressure. That's all I've heard.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen while we talk. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur, and the rate's about ninety-six sitting here. Blood pressure is one eighteen over seventy-four, oxygen ninety-eight percent. Lungs are clear, no wheeze.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-six, like, bad? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): A bit quick for resting, not a danger number on its own. Working this through — heavy caffeine, nicotine, spells at night and before exams or meetings, no chest pain. My impression is this may be sinus tachycardia stirred up by the coffee and the vaping.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I also can't rule out an arrhythmia, or a thyroid issue. That's a working impression, not a final label, and it does not sound like a heart attack.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. So my heart's not, um, failing or something.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think so. You're young and the exam is reassuring. I do want an ECG before you leave today, and thyroid bloodwork, a TSH and a free T4.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Today? I've got a seminar at four. Um, I can stay a little.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): ECG here before you go, and the lab order is in — today or first thing tomorrow is fine. If the palpitations haven't settled in a few weeks, we might do a Holter monitor, but I'm not ordering that now. If the shortness of breath doesn't ease up, we might get a chest x-ray, only in that case.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): For now, drop the energy drinks and cut the coffee way back. When an episode starts, try slow breathing, in for four counts and out for six. I'll see you back in two weeks to go over the results. If you faint or get chest pain, come in sooner than that.

omissions.text: Episodes last about 5 to 20 minutes, per patient estimate.
Shortness of breath usually starts after the heart racing, though sometimes they begin together; patient was uncertain.
At night the episodes occur while still awake lying in bed, not waking from sleep gasping.
Buspirone was prescribed for nerves but was never filled and never taken, so it is not a current medication.
Patient reported one-time use of a roommate's Adderall months ago before a final; not prescribed and not repeated.
Doctor documented a real disagreement/uncertainty: patient denies stress/anxiety as a trigger, but doctor noted the timing with meetings still nags at them.
Doctor stated the presentation does not sound like a heart attack.
